stories.headline: Update: U.S. Strikes Over 80 Iran Targets, Reimposed Sanctions as Iran Threatens 'Crushing Response'
stories.summary:
U.S. Central Command announced it completed a new round of offensive strikes against Iran on Tuesday, hitting more than 80 targets including oil infrastructure on Kharg Island, port facilities at Bandar Abbas and Sirik, and Qeshm Island. The strikes came in retaliation for Iranian attacks on commercial vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz. Simultaneously, the Trump administration revoked a sanctions waiver for Iranian oil sales, reimposing economic pressure it had eased as part of last month's interim ceasefire agreement.

Iran's top military command, Khatam al-Anbiya Central Headquarters, responded in the early hours of Wednesday warning it would deliver a 'crushing response to the US aggression.' Iran's chief nuclear negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf accused Washington of violating their memorandum of understanding, declaring 'the era of bullying and extortion is over.' Air raid sirens sounded in Bahrain — home to the U.S. Navy's Fifth Fleet — as Iran's warning spread, with the Bahraini government urging citizens to seek shelter.

The escalation has put the fragile ceasefire under severe strain. Regional sources told CNN that some Gulf allies were urgently sending messages to both Washington and Tehran urging restraint. The strikes and sanctions move came as Iran was in the midst of state funeral ceremonies for Supreme Leader Khamenei, adding a charged symbolic dimension to the military exchange.

The clashes form a backdrop to the NATO summit in Ankara, Turkey, where President Trump and allied leaders gathered Tuesday. European allies, many of whom declined to provide bases or forces for U.S. operations against Iran, face renewed friction with Washington over the conflict even as they sought to address Trump's longstanding defense-spending complaints.

stories.headline: China Tests Submarine-Launched ICBM in Pacific; U.S. Condemns Launch
stories.summary:
The Trump administration on Tuesday condemned China's test launch of an unarmed intercontinental ballistic missile fired from a submarine in the Pacific Ocean, calling the event 'of great concern.' A State Department statement declared: 'At a time when the United States is working harder than ever to prevent nuclear proliferation, China is doing the opposite.' The test occurred Monday and drew a swift public rebuke from Washington.

Analysts said the submarine-launched ICBM test may signal the beginning of more regular Pacific launches as China works to modernize and expand its nuclear arsenal. The ability to fire ICBMs from submarines adds a survivable second-strike capability that significantly complicates U.S. and allied defense planning in the Indo-Pacific region. Governments already wary of China's military buildup, including Japan, Australia, and South Korea, are expected to view the test as further evidence of accelerating Chinese nuclear ambitions.

The test comes at a particularly fraught moment in U.S.-China relations, with Washington simultaneously engaged in military operations against Iran, managing tensions at the NATO summit, and navigating ongoing trade and technology disputes with Beijing. Arms control experts noted that the U.S. and China have no bilateral nuclear risk-reduction framework comparable to the agreements Washington maintained with Moscow during the Cold War, leaving fewer formal channels to manage escalation risks.

The condemnation was covered by Bloomberg and The Hill, with limited but substantive sourcing given the inherent significance of a submarine-launched ICBM test by a major nuclear power. The Pentagon has not detailed whether it tracked the launch in real time or whether it triggered any immediate military response.

stories.headline: Update: U.S. Launches New Strikes on Iran as Hormuz Shipping Attacks Threaten Ceasefire
stories.summary:
The U.S. military launched fresh strikes against Iranian targets early Wednesday after three merchant ships were struck by projectiles in the Strait of Hormuz, the latest exchange threatening an interim ceasefire deal between the two countries. U.S. Central Command said the strikes were intended to "impose heavy costs" for targeting commercial shipping and called Iran's actions "a clear violation of the ceasefire." Iranian state media reported explosions in Qeshm and Bandar Abbas.

The renewed hostilities are the most significant development since the interim deal was reached, with U.S. officials revoking a previously issued license in the hours after the tanker attacks. The strikes came while President Trump was in Ankara, Turkey, attending the NATO summit, adding diplomatic complexity to an already volatile situation. Negotiations aimed at fully reopening the strait, curbing Iran's nuclear program, and reaching a permanent end to the war launched February 28 remain ongoing but increasingly fragile.

A similar cycle of Iranian shipping attacks and U.S. retaliation occurred late last month, but this round is seen as more serious given the scale and timing. The Strait of Hormuz is a critical chokepoint for global oil flows, and continued instability there carries broad economic consequences. Iran's new leadership, still consolidating power following Ayatollah Khamenei's death, has not issued a formal public response.

stories.headline: Manhattan High-Rise Near Grand Central Remains Unstable After Columns Buckle During Renovation
stories.summary:
A 37-story Manhattan office building being converted into luxury apartments buckled on two columns on its 21st and 22nd floors Tuesday morning, causing floors between the 21st and 26th stories to sag and prompting evacuations of the building and surrounding structures near Grand Central Terminal. New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Fire Chief John Esposito said the building remained unstable and was being monitored by drones to avoid sending personnel inside. A nearby school with approximately 400 students was among the evacuated buildings; officials reported no injuries.

The structure is the former global headquarters of pharmaceutical giant Pfizer and is undergoing what its architectural firm, Gensler, has called the largest office-to-residential conversion in New York City history, with more than 1,600 planned apartment units. City officials said engineers would need to install emergency beams and columns to stabilize the compromised sections before workers could safely enter. Fire officials assessed the risk as a potential "localized collapse" rather than a total structural failure.

The incident drew attention to the broader wave of office-to-residential conversion projects underway in major U.S. cities. Streets in the immediate vicinity of the Chrysler Building and Grand Central remained closed to pedestrians and vehicles as of Tuesday morning, with officials describing the situation as a "minute-by-minute assessment."

stories.headline: Federal Judge Quashes DOJ Subpoena Seeking Names of Fulton County 2020 Election Workers
stories.summary:
A federal judge in Georgia on Tuesday quashed a grand jury subpoena through which the Department of Justice had sought the names and personal contact information of election workers who administered the 2020 presidential vote in Fulton County. U.S. District Judge William Ray, a Trump appointee, found that the subpoena was improper and that it was too late to bring criminal charges, casting serious doubt on the DOJ's effort to reinvestigate Trump's unsubstantiated claims of widespread fraud in that race.

The ruling represents a significant setback for the Trump administration's DOJ, which had revived scrutiny of the 2020 Georgia results. Critics of the probe, including Democratic officials and election law advocates, had warned that compelling election workers to hand over personal information could expose them to harassment or intimidation. Supporters of the investigation argued it was a legitimate effort to audit the integrity of voter rolls and election administration.

The case adds to a pattern of judicial pushback against DOJ election-related subpoenas; a separate federal judge recently dismissed a DOJ lawsuit seeking detailed voter data from Maryland. Fulton County officials welcomed the ruling, with one attorney noting it "protects the privacy of vulnerable individuals." The DOJ has not publicly commented on whether it will appeal.

stories.headline: Cyclospora Parasite Outbreak Surges Across Multiple U.S. States, CDC Investigating
stories.summary:
A sharp rise in cyclosporiasis infections has prompted federal and state health officials to launch investigations across more than a dozen states. As of July 7, Michigan alone has reported more than 708 confirmed cases — compared to roughly 170 just days earlier and a typical annual total of about 50. Ohio has logged at least 170 cases since late June, with Indiana, New York, and North Carolina each reporting more than 100 additional infections in recent weeks.

Cyclosporiasis is caused by a microscopic parasite, Cyclospora cayetanensis, that spreads through contaminated food and water, typically fresh produce. The illness causes prolonged, watery diarrhea and can require hospitalization. Nationwide, at least 20 people have been hospitalized across 17 states since May 1, though no deaths have been reported. The infected range in age from 5 to 86.

The CDC, working alongside the FDA and local health departments, said there is currently no evidence of a single multi-state outbreak linking all cases to one source, and no specific food, grower, or supplier has been identified. All known cases appear to be domestically acquired, with no international travel reported among those infected.

Health officials in Michigan described the spike as "sudden and large" and are urging residents who experience symptoms to seek medical care. Cyclosporiasis is a seasonal illness that typically peaks between May and August, but the scale of this year's surge has raised concern among public health authorities.

stories.headline: Rahm Emanuel to Denounce Netanyahu in Tel Aviv Speech, Calling U.S.-Israel Relationship at a 'Crossroads'
stories.summary:
Rahm Emanuel, a potential 2028 Democratic presidential candidate and longtime centrist defender of Israel, is set to deliver a pointed speech at Tel Aviv University on Wednesday in which he will call for significant changes to the U.S.-Israel relationship and directly criticize Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. In remarks obtained in advance by the Associated Press, Emanuel plans to say the relationship "cannot stand or survive as it has been" without new direction, and that Israel's military campaign in Gaza has been "reckless and careless in the treatment of Palestinian life."

Emanuel's proposals include imposing sanctions on Israelis who attack Palestinian civilians, cutting U.S. subsidies to Israel's defense budget, and treating Israel's arms purchases under the same terms applied to other allied nations. He stopped short of calling Israel's actions genocide, saying the term should not be politicized, but said he was willing to engage in that debate.

The speech reflects a broader leftward shift in Democratic public opinion on Israel. A new AP-NORC survey found that approximately 58 percent of Democrats believe the U.S. is "too supportive" of Israel, up from 45 percent in January 2024, and about half of Democrats believe Israel has committed genocide against Palestinians during the Gaza conflict.

Emanuel's remarks are notable in part because he has historically been a strong defender of the U.S.-Israel alliance. His decision to deliver this address in Tel Aviv rather than Washington underscores the political significance of the moment and his apparent effort to position himself as a new voice on Middle East policy within the Democratic Party ahead of 2028.

stories.headline: U.S. Citizen Sues ICE, Claims Officers Visited His Home Over Critical Email to Agency Head
stories.summary:
A U.S. citizen from Rochester, New York, has filed a lawsuit against Immigration and Customs Enforcement alleging that federal agents showed up at his home to deliver a warning after he sent a critical email to the then-acting director of ICE. David Streever was traveling in Finland in June when two federal officers appeared at his door and presented his wife with a notice stating that an email he had sent months earlier had been deemed a threat. The lawsuit was filed Monday in Washington, D.C.

Streever had sent the email in January to Todd Lyons, then ICE's acting director, following the fatal shooting of Minneapolis resident Renee Good by an immigration officer during an anti-ICE protest. The three-paragraph email called Lyons "a monstrous human being" and compared him to a senior Nazi official, stating that he "will never know peace." Streever's attorneys, from the Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression, argue the message is clearly protected political speech under the First Amendment.

DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin's office disputed the characterization, stating that "any allegation DHS and its components are attempting to 'squash' free speech is categorically FALSE" and that anyone who threatens law enforcement officers "will face the consequences." ICE previously declined to comment, citing an ongoing investigation.

Streever is one of at least two upstate New York residents who received federal warnings following online criticism of ICE. Civil liberties advocates say the case illustrates a pattern of using federal law enforcement presence to deter constitutionally protected criticism of the government; the government maintains the warning was a legitimate response to language it considered threatening.

stories.headline: India's Ram Temple Overhauls Leadership After Alleged Theft of Tens of Millions in Donations
stories.summary:
The trust overseeing India's grand Ram temple in Ayodhya has accepted the resignation of its general secretary and announced a leadership overhaul following allegations that tens of millions of rupees in donations were stolen. The shake-up came after the trust's first meeting since the allegations surfaced last month. Ayodhya police have registered an embezzlement case naming eight people, all of whom have been arrested and are under questioning.

The Shri Ram Janmabhoomi Teerth Kshetra Trust, which manages the politically and religiously significant temple, initially denied wrongdoing. However, following an interim report from a state-appointed Special Investigation Team, authorities moved forward with the criminal case. The trust collected approximately 5.82 billion rupees ($61 million) in donations through March 2026, with a former accounts supervisor alleging that more than 70 million rupees ($739,000) may have gone missing.

The temple, inaugurated by Prime Minister Narendra Modi in January 2024, has become one of India's most important pilgrimage sites, drawing an estimated 50 million visitors annually. It was built on the site of a 16th-century mosque demolished by Hindu mobs in 1992 — an event that triggered nationwide riots killing nearly 2,000 people — making the temple one of the country's most politically charged religious institutions.

Opposition parties have seized on the allegations to question the ruling BJP government's stewardship of the site. The trust has created a new CEO position and appointed a retired forest officer and member of the RSS — the Hindu nationalist umbrella organization aligned with Modi's party — as interim general secretary. Petitions seeking a court-monitored federal investigation have been filed in both a state high court and the Supreme Court.

stories.headline: Nigel Farage Resigns as MP, Triggers By-Election Amid Financial Scandal
stories.summary:
British populist leader Nigel Farage resigned Tuesday as a Member of Parliament for Clacton, triggering a special by-election in what he framed as a direct appeal to voters amid a parliamentary investigation into undisclosed financial gifts. Farage said he would stand in the by-election himself, calling it "a people versus the establishment" contest. His resignation suspends two ongoing parliamentary inquiries into donations he received, including from a convicted criminal.

Farage has been accused of violating British parliamentary disclosure rules by failing to report financial gifts. Outgoing Prime Minister Keir Starmer dismissed the move as a "desperate stunt," saying Farage was "up to his neck in sleaze." Farage denied any wrongdoing, saying the voters of Clacton — not a parliamentary standards committee — should judge him.

The stakes are substantial for British politics. Farage's Reform UK party has topped national opinion polls for over a year and performed strongly in recent local elections, contributing to pressure that led to Starmer's own resignation. If Farage wins his seat back, he could emerge as the leading opposition figure to incoming Labour leader Andy Burnham. If he loses, he would be barred from becoming prime minister.

The gamble reflects the high-wire nature of Farage's political brand, built on anti-establishment populism and Brexit. Supporters see the move as bold and principled; critics view it as an attempt to escape accountability by bypassing the formal parliamentary oversight process.

stories.headline: Lawsuit Alleges Trump Administration Shared Iranian Asylum Seekers' Files With Tehran
stories.summary:
The Iranian American Legal Defense Fund filed a federal lawsuit Tuesday alleging the Trump administration has been sharing confidential immigration files of Iranian asylum seekers — including their asylum applications — directly with the Iranian government. The complaint, filed in Washington, D.C., claims ICE held monthly meetings with Iranian government officials and shared document packages containing case details, despite federal regulations prohibiting disclosure of asylum application information to the country from which a person fled.

The suit says more than 100 Iranians have been deported during the Trump administration, and that many of those in ICE custody are pro-democracy activists, religious minorities, or LGBTQ individuals who face persecution, torture, or death if identified by the Iranian government. According to the complaint, Iranian officials also met with detainees at ICE facilities without their consent, and those officials demonstrated knowledge of the detainees' specific asylum cases. The nonprofit Public Citizen is representing the plaintiffs.

The Department of Homeland Security and the State Department did not immediately respond to requests for comment. A DHS statement on a related matter denied any attempt to suppress free speech, though it did not address the asylum-sharing allegations specifically. The complaint also alleges the information-sharing continued even after the outbreak of direct U.S.-Iran hostilities on February 28.

The case raises significant legal and human rights questions about the limits of immigration enforcement coordination with adversarial governments during wartime. Civil liberties advocates say the alleged conduct could expose deportees to life-threatening consequences upon return to Iran, while the administration has broadly argued that deportation coordination with receiving governments is a necessary logistical requirement.

stories.headline: Tornadoes and Severe Storms Kill at Least 11 in China's Hubei Province
stories.summary:
At least 11 people were killed and more than 300 injured after severe thunderstorms and rare tornadoes struck multiple cities in China's Hubei province on Tuesday, according to state media. The storms caused widespread damage to thousands of buildings across the neighboring cities of Ezhou and Huanggang, with videos of the twisters circulating widely online. Local authorities have launched rescue and relief operations.

A student in Huanggang told the BBC the event initially appeared to be an ordinary thunderstorm before objects began flying through the air and glass shattered dormitory windows. "It wasn't until everything had finally stopped that I realized I had just lived through a disaster," the student said. Tornadoes are rare in the region; state media reported the last recorded occurrence was in 2021.

The death toll and scale of structural damage place this event in the category of a significant natural disaster for a densely populated region of central China. Rescue operations are ongoing and casualty figures may rise as authorities assess the full extent of damage across the affected cities.

stories.headline: Update: LNG Tanker Struck and Ablaze in Strait of Hormuz as U.S.-Iran Talks Remain on Hold
stories.summary:
A liquefied natural gas tanker was struck by a projectile and caught fire early Tuesday in the Strait of Hormuz off the coast of Oman, according to the British military. Iranian state television acknowledged the attack, saying the vessel had ignored warnings, without directly claiming responsibility. Tehran has repeatedly declared that only its approved shipping route through the strait is safe, and has been suspected in similar attacks on vessels using an alternate route near the Omani shore.

The attack comes as U.S.-Iran negotiations aimed at fully reopening the strait, rolling back Iran's nuclear program, and ending the ongoing conflict remain stalled. American officials said talks appeared to be on hold pending the burial of Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, who was killed at the outset of the war that began February 28. Tens of thousands of mourners gathered in Qom, Iran, for funeral services Tuesday.

Previous attacks in the Strait of Hormuz have triggered retaliatory U.S. strikes on Iran, which in turn led to Iranian attacks on Gulf Arab states, raising the risk of further escalation. In peacetime, roughly a fifth of all globally traded oil and natural gas passed through the narrow channel, making its security a matter of acute concern for world energy markets.

The incident underscores the fragility of any interim arrangements in the region and complicates diplomatic efforts to stabilize the Persian Gulf. No immediate claim of responsibility was issued, and the fate of the tanker's crew was not immediately reported.

stories.headline: Wildfire in Southern France Forces Evacuation of 10,000 as European Heatwave Intensifies
stories.summary:
A rapidly spreading wildfire in the foothills of the French Pyrenees near Perpignan has forced the evacuation of more than 10,000 residents from over a dozen towns and villages, French authorities said Tuesday. The blaze, centered near Trévillach, has burned at least 4,600 hectares as of Tuesday morning, with Interior Minister Laurent Nunez warning that deteriorating conditions and strong winds could drive the fire further. Residents described the fire advancing to within 300 meters of homes at terrifying speed.

The European Commission announced it would dispatch four firefighting aircraft from Cyprus and Sweden to assist French emergency services. The fires have also affected northeastern Spain, where more than 2,200 hectares of the Les Gavarres nature reserve have been destroyed and 500 people were evacuated from the Sierra de Espadan national park in Castellon province.

The wildfires are unfolding amid a severe early-summer heatwave that has already proved deadly across Europe. Temperatures exceeded 40 degrees Celsius in parts of Portugal and Spain, and forecasters warned the heat could persist into next week with little rainfall expected. A record-breaking heatwave in June was linked to at least 2,025 excess deaths in France, 1,222 in Belgium, and roughly 480 in the Netherlands.

The Tour de France was also affected, with race organizers urging spectators to avoid the final 40 kilometers of the third stage and reducing the convoy of team vehicles to allow emergency access. Climate scientists have linked the increasing frequency and severity of European heatwaves and associated wildfires to long-term climate change.

stories.headline: Monaco Bombing Suspect Found Dead in Ukraine; Military Intelligence Officer Confesses to Murder
stories.summary:
Anastasiia Berezovska, the Ukrainian woman suspected of carrying out a parcel bombing in Monaco that seriously injured a sanctioned Ukrainian businessman and his family on June 29, has been found dead in Ukraine with gunshot wounds to the head, the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) announced Tuesday. Two suspects have been detained in connection with her killing: a former law enforcement officer and a serving officer in Ukraine's Ministry of Defence military intelligence directorate, the latter of whom confessed to the murder.

Berezovska had returned to Ukraine two days after the Monaco attack, where investigators say she was in contact with both men, who had allegedly transferred funds to her crypto and bank accounts prior to the bombing. During a search of the former law enforcement officer's residence, police said they discovered a basement room described as resembling a torture chamber.

The Monaco attack targeted Vadym Yermolaiev, identified by local media as a real estate developer ranked among Ukraine's wealthiest individuals, his partner, and his 13-year-old son. All three were injured, two seriously, when a package exploded in the entrance of an apartment building. Monaco authorities had issued an Interpol red notice for Berezovska, and European police conducted searches in Germany before her body was found.

The case has drawn intense scrutiny in Ukraine given the involvement of an active military intelligence officer. The SBU said its investigation was proceeding with the direct involvement of intelligence directorate chief Oleg Ivashchenko, and that authorities were working to identify additional suspects.

stories.headline: Update: Marine Le Pen Appeal Verdict Due Tuesday; French Presidential Race Hangs in Balance
stories.summary:
A Paris appeals court is set to deliver its verdict Tuesday at 13:30 local time on whether to uphold Marine Le Pen's embezzlement conviction, a ruling that will determine whether France's leading presidential contender can stand in the 2027 election. Le Pen was originally convicted in March 2025 of embezzling €1.4 million in European Parliament funds to pay National Rally party employees, and was sentenced to five years barred from public office along with a four-year prison term.

If the appeals court upholds the conviction, Le Pen — who currently leads presidential polls — would be barred from the race. Her 29-year-old lieutenant Jordan Bardella would likely stand in her place. If the court overturns or reduces the sentence sufficiently, she would be free to run, effectively firing the starting gun on the presidential campaign with the first round scheduled for April 18, 2027.

Le Pen has portrayed herself as a victim of politically motivated justice, arguing she received unequal treatment compared to other politicians found guilty of fraud. Prosecutors, however, have maintained that she was at the heart of a systematic fake-jobs scheme and are seeking the original five-year ban to stand. The verdict is among the most consequential judicial decisions in recent French political history.

stories.headline: Explosions Injure 18 in Damascus During French President Macron's Visit
stories.summary:
Two explosive devices detonated in central Damascus on Tuesday, injuring 18 people including four police officers, Syrian state media reported. The blasts occurred approximately 125 meters from the Four Seasons hotel where French President Emmanuel Macron had been staying during a landmark diplomatic visit — the first by a European Union leader since Ahmed al-Sharaa came to power following the fall of the Assad regime in December 2024.

Syrian state news agency SANA said security forces had detected the devices and that they detonated while specialised units were attempting to defuse them. One device was concealed in a parked vehicle, the other in a rubbish bin. Macron's office confirmed he was safe and had not heard the explosions; he continued his visit, writing on social media that "nothing can smother the aspiration of Syrian women and men to live in a fully sovereign, safe, pluralistic, and united Syria."

The attack underscores the severe security challenges facing Syria's new government as it seeks international legitimacy and reconstruction investment. The Islamic State group has claimed a series of attacks on government targets in recent months, including a bomb blast at a Damascus café on July 1 that killed nine people. Macron was in Damascus for talks focused on Syria's political transition and economic reconstruction before heading to the NATO summit in Ankara.

stories.headline: Update: Trump Arrives at NATO Summit in Ankara Angered Over Allies' Refusal to Back Iran War
stories.summary:
President Trump arrived in Ankara on Tuesday for the annual NATO summit carrying unresolved anger toward allies who declined to grant overflight rights or open military bases during U.S. operations against Iran, according to reporting from Axios and The Hill. The grievance has deepened longstanding Trump skepticism about the alliance's value, and officials say he intends allies to be aware of his displeasure during the summit.

The summit's agenda is dominated by defense spending targets, with NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte pressing members for "clear, concrete and credible" plans to meet 2030 goals. Allies have unveiled $12 billion in defense procurement deals — including next-generation drones and surveillance aircraft — in part to demonstrate responsiveness to Trump's demands. Several European nations are also advancing a joint defense financing initiative.

Adding complexity, Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu called Trump ahead of the summit to complain about Turkish President Erdoğan's anti-Israel rhetoric and to urge Trump not to sell weapons systems that would modernize Turkey's air force. Turkey's re-entry into the F-35 program has emerged as a flashpoint, with Republican critics and Israel opposing restoring access while Ankara retains Russian air defense systems. Ukraine's President Zelensky is also attending, seeking continued support amid an ongoing interceptor shortage following Russia's massive missile strike on Kyiv.

stories.headline: Khamenei Funeral Procession Draws Thousands in Tehran; Red Flags Signal Vengeance
stories.summary:
Hundreds of thousands of mourners lined the streets of Tehran on Tuesday for the funeral procession of Iran's late Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, who was killed along with several family members in U.S. strikes earlier this year. The coffins were carried along a 10-kilometer route through the capital in a carefully choreographed event that Iran's state broadcaster said would last 10 to 12 hours.

The procession was suffused with political symbolism: red flags representing a pledge of vengeance were prominent throughout the crowds, and mourners were seen throwing rocks at a poster bearing President Trump's image. Anti-Trump and anti-American messages were visible throughout the procession route, reflecting the state-directed tone of the weeklong funeral.

The mass public ceremony marks one of the most significant moments of political transition in Iran in decades. With Khamenei dead and a new leadership structure taking shape, the funeral serves as both a mourning ritual and a political statement about the Islamic Republic's intentions and continuity. The event is being watched closely by U.S. and allied intelligence services for signals about Iran's posture ahead of ongoing negotiations.
